title: A week on two rivers
hook: Thoreau's first book remembers a boat trip with John (A Week on the Concord and Merrimack Rivers)

segments.voice: Yesterday, his brother John: a small cut, then lockjaw, and a grief slow to find words. Your line was John.

A small boat sits at the edge of the Concord River. Two brothers built it themselves, and Henry describes it lovingly: shaped like a fisherman's dory, painted green below, with a border of blue. They load food, a tent and something to sleep on, then push off downstream toward a second river. Years later, after John was gone, Henry wrote the trip down. It became his first book, with a title as plain as a ship's log: A Week on the Concord and Merrimack Rivers.
screen: `A HOMEMADE BOAT.` → `TWO BROTHERS PUSH OFF.` → `LATER, A BOOK.`

segments.voice: First, a book made of days. The chapters aren't numbered. They're named: Saturday, Sunday, Monday, and on through Friday. Each is a day on the water. You row with the brothers, camp on the bank, wake to fog. The calendar becomes the shape of a memory. Second, a river that wanders. The boat goes forward, but the book keeps drifting. A bend in the river turns into pages on friendship. A quiet Sunday turns into thoughts on books and faith, and on scriptures from more than one tradition. Then he's back at the oars, describing a fish, a lock, a farmer on the shore. Some readers find this maddening. Others find it the whole point: this is how a mind moves on a slow day outside. Third, the brother in the boat. John is there throughout, rowing, pitching the tent, sharing the watch, yet he mostly stays folded inside the word we. At the front of the book, Henry set a short verse to the one who sailed with him, asking him, wherever he now sails, to be his muse, his brother. The trip is told as an adventure. Underneath, it's a remembering. Fourth, why a small journey matters. They didn't cross an ocean. They went up a river near home. Thoreau treats it as worth a whole book, because who you travel with, and how closely you look, can make a short distance enormous. A week, two rivers, two brothers. That's enough.
screen: `CHAPTERS NAMED FOR DAYS.` · `A RIVER THAT WANDERS.` · `THE BROTHER IN THE BOAT.` · `A SHORT DISTANCE, ENORMOUS.` · then, large: `A WEEK ON TWO RIVERS.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one short trip you once made with someone: a drive to the coast, a walk to school, a ride to the store with a parent. Go along it slowly: where you started, what you passed, what they said or didn't say. You don't have to make it meaningful; just ride along it again, and notice who was in the boat with you.
A week on two rivers. Thoreau's first book: a boat trip with his brother John, told day by day, wandering into big thoughts, and quietly remembering. Today's word.
